originalText: `#searchLiteral` builds the LIKE pattern as `'%' || @__query__ || '%'` without escaping SQLite LIKE metacharacters (`%` and `_`) in the bound value. A caller searching for a literal `%` will match every document; `_` matches any single character. The documented contract is "case-insensitive substring scan" — exact substring, not wildcard. For the primary use case (UUIDs) this is harmless, but it silently diverges from the documented contract for any query containing these characters. Fix with `REPLACE`-based escaping and an `ESCAPE` clause, or switch to `INSTR`-based matching. Also add a test: `index.search('%', { mode: 'literal' })` should return only documents whose content literally contains `%`, not all documents.
evidence:
#searchLiteral calls #escapeLikePattern(query) at line 558 before binding
the query parameter. The escapeLikePattern helper at lines 535-540 replaces
`\`, `%`, and `_` with escaped versions. The LIKE clause at line 552 includes
`ESCAPE '\\'`, enabling literal matching. A query containing `%` will match
only documents with that character, not all documents.

originalText: `#buildParams` seeds the param object with the internal sentinels `__query__` and `__limit__` first, then overwrites any key with a matching filter-column name. Because `IDENTIFIER_PATTERN` (`/^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$/`) permits names like `__query__` and `__limit__`, a caller who declares a metadata column with either of those names and applies a filter on it will silently replace the FTS MATCH expression (or the row cap) with the filter's value — producing wrong results without any error. This touches all three call sites where `#buildParams` feeds a named-parameter dict into `#searchFullText` (line ~513) and `#searchLiteral` (line ~568). Fix: reject the two sentinel names explicitly in `#validateIdentifier` or at the top of `#validateFilters`; or switch to a more uniquely namespaced prefix (e.g. `__m3l_query__`, `__m3l_limit__`) that is even less likely to collide.
evidence:
#buildParams at lines 590-604 seeds the param object with `__query__` and
`__limit__` at lines 597-598, then overwrites with filter column values
(lines 600-602). There is no guard in the constructor or #validateIdentifier
preventing a metadata column from being named `__query__` or `__limit__`.
A caller declaring such a column would silently replace the FTS expression
or row limit with the filter value.

originalText: The "ANSI-aware width" test sets `const colored = "[31mABC[39m]"` — that string lacks the `\x1b` escape prefix, so it is *not* a real ANSI sequence. `stringWidth` counts all those bracket characters as visible glyphs, making the column width 12, not 3. Because both formatted outputs end up with the same 16-char column width (driven by `"wide-plain-label"`), the `expect(coloredLineLengths).toEqual(plainLineLengths)` assertion happens to pass, but it does not exercise the ANSI-aware code path at all. Replace `"[31mABC[39m"` with `"\x1b[31mABC\x1b[39m"` (real escape codes) so the test actually validates that `stringWidth` discounts the invisible ANSI bytes when computing column layout.
evidence: The ANSI-aware width test at line 1323-1353 now uses real ANSI escape codes: `const colored = "\x1b[31mABC\x1b[39m";` at line 1326. The finding claimed it used a version with no escape prefix, which would not exercise the ANSI-aware path. The current code has the correct escape sequences (\x1b prefix) so stringWidth can properly discount invisible bytes.

originalText: the human-mode "all steps passed" banner is gated on `sequenceCompleted = steps.every((s) => s.ok)`, where `s.ok` tracks only the child's exit code (per the `runJsonStep` doc comment around line 401, this is intentional so a step that reports errors via its JSON payload but still exits 0 doesn't halt the sequence). Several steps in this chain never call `process.exit(1)` at all — e.g. `bin/gen-doc-counts.mjs` (step 3, "Doc counts regen") calls `reporter.error(...)` in at least two places but has no `process.exit` call anywhere, so it always exits 0 even when it recorded a structural error. Concrete scenario: `docs/implementation-status.md` is missing its `GENERATED IMPLEMENTED-LIST` markers → `gen-doc-counts.mjs` reports an error but exits 0 → that step is recorded `ok: true` → `sequenceCompleted` stays `true` through the remaining steps → the script prints `✓  /syncing-docs: all 14 step(s) passed.`, even though the forwarded error flips the top-level `reporter.ok` to `false` and `process.exit(sequenceCompleted && finalPayload.ok ? 0 : 1)` on line 606 exits with code `1` moments later. A human running `pnpm sync:docs` interactively sees a green success banner directly contradicted by the process's own exit code. Net effect is scoped: the exit code (the actual gate) and the JSON payload's `ok`/`errors` (what an agent/CI would actually check) are both still correct — only the human-readable summary line is misleading — but it undercuts the tool's stated purpose of "one go/no-go verdict" for anyone reading the console output. `sequenceCompleted`/the `reporter.succeed` condition should also account for accumulated step `errors`, not just `ok`.

pass this check, printing a success banner even though `finalPayload.ok` is

A journal line like `"Not blocked anymore, wrapping up"` or `"Nothing remaining"` still matches `\b(?:blocked|...|remaining)\b` and classifies as `"pending"`, which can surface as a spurious `outstandingPending` item — producing a false "resume with punch-list: nothing remaining" recommendation instead of `"none"`. originalText: the dispatcher's template-conflict check and the writer's template resolution disagree on what "set" means: `resolveTemplateText` treats *any* non-`undefined` `templateBody`/`templateUrl` as a conflict, while `resolveTemplateBody` (`write-stack.ts:118`) only honours *string* values. With `{"stackName":"s","templateUrl":null}` plus `--template t.yaml`, the run throws a conflict error even though `write-stack` would have ignored the `null` and used the template file — the two sites should share one predicate.
evidence: The dispatcher's `resolveTemplateText` at lines 144-146 checks raw record values: `record["templateBody"] !== undefined || record["templateUrl"] !== undefined`, treating any non-undefined value as a conflict. The writer's `resolveTemplateBody` in write-stack.ts:52 calls `reader.optionalStringField`, which only honors string values. A record with `{templateUrl: null}` would trigger a conflict error in the dispatcher but would be treated as absent in the writer (the reader would throw on non-string, but never gets called). The two sites disagree on what "set" means.

originalText: `gateOperation` builds the confirmation description from the *presence* of `raw.nodegroup`, not from the operation's own resource kind, so a cluster-level destructive operation run with a stale/preset `nodegroup` value prompts `delete-cluster cluster 'c' nodegroup 'n'` — naming a nodegroup in the one message an operator reads before approving a cluster deletion. The `ecs-ops` precedent (`scripts/ecs-ops/src/steps/run-ecs-ops.ts:197`) builds the description per-operation from that operation's resolved identity instead. Reachable today: the `MUTATING_OPERATIONS` case in `tests/run-eks-ops.test.ts` passes both `cluster` and `nodegroup` for `delete-cluster`.
evidence: The `prepare` function builds the confirmation description by checking raw.nodegroup presence (line 298-300) regardless of operation type. For a cluster-level operation like delete-cluster run with a stale nodegroup value, the description would incorrectly name the nodegroup. The description should be built per-operation from that operation's resolved identity (e.g., cluster-only for delete-cluster, both for delete-nodegroup), not from config presence.

originalText: `escapeChoiceItem` classifies a *bare* element as choice-shaped whenever `Value` itself carries a `value` key (e.g. `M3LChoices<{ value: string; label: string }>`), and then forwards only `item.value` to the adapter — collapsing the element the caller expected back. With the real `@inquirer/prompts` adapter this matches pre-existing behavior (inquirer applies the same `"value" in choice` discrimination), so it is not a regression there; but `M3LPromptAdapter` is a public injection point, and a custom adapter now receives the collapsed object where it previously received the raw element. The new docs assert this cannot happen — `docs/reference/core/prompt.md:70` ("the resolved `value` a caller receives on selection is **always** the original, unescaped value") and the class `@remarks` at `M3LPrompt.ts:207` ("transparent to the caller"). Either narrow those claims to inquirer-shaped adapters, or add the `Value extends { value: … }` case to the helper's TSDoc; there is no test pinning it either way.
evidence: When `Value extends { value: ... }` (e.g., `M3LChoices<{ value: string; label: string }>`), escapeChoiceItem's isChoiceLike check at line 157 classifies a bare element like `{ value: "x", label: "X" }` as choice-shaped (it has a "value" property per the `in` operator at line 127), then returns only `item.value` at line 159, collapsing the element. The class-level remarks at line 217 claim "the resolved `value` a caller receives on selection is **always** the original, unescaped value" (transparent to caller), but a custom M3LPromptAdapter receives the collapsed form. No test covers this case; the contract is stated but unverified for this edge case.

originalText: the new `toJSON` branch recurses through `canonicalizeValue`, which re-applies the `toJSON` check to the result; `JSON.stringify` applies `toJSON` only once per value and then serializes the result structurally. A value whose `toJSON` returns itself (`const o = { toJSON: () => o }`) recurses forever and escapes as a raw `RangeError` instead of the `M3LError(ERR_INVALID_ARGUMENT)` `json.md:118` promises for self-referential input — `JSON.stringify` returns `"{}"` for the same input. `path` does not catch it because each `toJSON()` call can yield a fresh object identity. Adding the receiver to `path` around the `toJSON` recursion (or serializing the result without re-checking `toJSON`) closes it.
evidence:
Line 141 calls `canonicalizeValue(value.toJSON(), path)` without tracking the
receiver object itself in `path` before recursing. A self-returning toJSON
like `const o = { toJSON: () => o }` produces infinite recursion escaping as
a raw RangeError, not the promised M3LError(ERR_INVALID_ARGUMENT). No test in
canonicalJson.test.ts covers self-referential toJSON.

originalText: the new regex `/from "\.\/([^/]+)\/index\.js";/gm` drops the `export` anchor entirely, so it matches *any* `from "./<name>/index.js";` clause — including `import` / `import type` lines. A future barrel that imports a submodule (e.g. to compose a union) without re-exporting it would satisfy the forward check, and the guard would silently pass a submodule that consumers cannot reach. Verified today's `src/core/index.ts` and `src/aws/index.ts` contain no `import` lines, so this is latent, not live. Anchoring to an export form (e.g. `/^(?!import\b).*from "\.\/([^/]+)\/index\.js";/gm`, which still matches both `export * from …` and a named block's `} from …` line) keeps the intended widening without the false positive.

The finding correctly notes this drops the `export` anchor, so an import-only line would match and register as proof of re-export when no re-export actually exists. originalText: the gate checks alias-vs-current-key but never alias-vs-alias, so the exact hazard it exists to prevent is still reachable. `legacyKeys` is derived from live rows (`impl:${slug(label)}`), not a frozen list, so a new row whose slugged label duplicates one in another `slug()`-using section produces two identical aliases; `indexItemsByKey` keeps only the first (`if (!byKey.has(legacy))`, section order friction → rollout → capability → hardening → cli → procedure → gated). Concrete case: add `A1` to the capability-deepening wave and its `impl:a1` alias is registered before the codified-procedure wave's — the existing issue carrying `<!-- m3l-hub-sync:impl:a1 -->` (really the procedure-wave A1) then resolves to the capability item, gets its title/body rewritten to the wrong item, and the procedure item is filed as a new issue. Today's corpus has 110 aliases with zero exact duplicates (only the five `impl:A#`/`impl:a#` case-variant pairs, which are harmless under case-sensitive marker matching), so this is latent, not live — but it is the same class of latent hazard the PR's own ADR Update argues should be fixed structurally rather than left to an accident. A fourth `kind` over duplicate aliases would close it.
evidence: The findKeyCollisions function checks for duplicate keys (lines 103-113), case-variant keys (lines 115-134), and legacy-shadow collisions where an alias matches another item's current key (lines 136-153). However, it never checks alias-vs-alias: whether a legacyKey from one item collides with a legacyKey from another item. Since legacyKeys are derived from slugged labels dynamically, two items with the same slugged label would both try to register the same alias, and only the first would win silently.

originalText: the CI step passes `github.event.pull_request.base.sha` (base-branch tip) into a two-dot range, and `bin/check-review-size.mjs:251` runs `git diff <base>..<head>`. The gate being reproduced measures `gh pr diff` (`.github/workflows/claude-pr-review.yml:230`), which is a merge-base/three-dot diff. Once `main` advances past the branch point, the two-dot range additionally contains the reverse-deltas of main-only commits, so this blocking step can report a larger number than the review gate and `process.exit(1)` (`bin/check-review-size.mjs:281`) on a PR the real gate would accept. `git diff <base>...<head>` (or resolving the merge-base as `resolveDefaultBase()` already does at `bin/check-review-size.mjs:168`) makes the two agree. Note the existing `Check exports semver labeling` step uses the same `base.sha` convention, but it compares content rather than counting bytes, so the divergence is harmless there.

The workflow's guard step uses `gh pr diff` which is a three-dot diff against the merge-base. Once main advances past the branch point, these diverge — the two-dot range includes main-only commits, so the gates step can report a larger byte count than the review gate allows.

deferring write-back errors, close() failure on the success path should

originalText:
the
  line ceiling is enforced one byte more loosely than the writer's, so a line
  the writer could never have produced reads back as genuine. `line` here
  excludes the terminating newline and is rejected only when
  `line.length > maxLineBytes`, while the writer measures content **plus** the
  newline (`append-only-writer.ts:313`, documented at
  `src/core/storage/append-only-read-types.ts:518` as "an entry serializing to
  exactly the ceiling is one byte too large"). At `maxLineBytes: 1024` the
  writer's largest possible content is 1023 bytes, but a 1024-byte content line
  is accepted on read — the same defect class the S2 regression suite
  (`tests/storage-append-only-read.test.ts:2467`) exists to close, off by one.
  The same asymmetry applies to the fragment check at
  `append-only-reader.ts:370`.
evidence:
At line 131, the check is `if (line.length + 1 > maxLineBytes)`, correctly
including the newline byte. The comment at lines 127-130 confirms this
aligns with the writer's ceiling (line in appendix-only-writer: content +
newline must fit). The same +1 check appears at line 146 for fragment
carry-over, resolving the one-byte asymmetry the finding described.

originalText:
the
  `finally` block swallows a `close()` failure with an empty `catch`, contrary
  to the no-silently-swallowed-errors rule. The read outcome legitimately takes
  precedence, but on the success path a failing `close()` disappears entirely
  with nothing surfaced.
evidence:
At lines 429-436, close() is called inside the try block (line 433) with
explicit error handling at lines 434-435 that throws via buildError. The
finally block (lines 450-454) only calls releaseAfterFailure if
`!closeAttempted`, preventing double-close and ensuring close failures on
the success path are surfaced as exceptions.

originalText: the close failure is discarded with no trace in two arms: when `primaryError` is `undefined` (early `break`), and when `chainSecondaryFailure` returns `false` (`chain-secondary-failure.ts:73` — no open slot within `MAX_CAUSE_CHAIN_WALK`, a hostile/frozen `.cause`, or a failed read-back). In both cases a descriptor the OS refused to release leaves zero signal, which is the outcome the no-silently-swallowed-errors rule targets. The success and chained arms are handled well; these two remainders need at least a diagnostic channel.
evidence:
In releaseAfterFailure, when close() throws, if primaryError is undefined
the error is silently swallowed (line 281 returns without throwing). If
chainSecondaryFailure returns false (no slot found, accessor error, or
read-back mismatch), the close error is also lost. These two cases leave
the descriptor release failure with zero diagnostic channel.

directory, not a file). The code then continues the upward walk and may return an

falls through without the defensive check.

originalText: the confirmation check only matches a string-valued `tool_result` block (`block?.content === "Structured output provided successfully"`). a string-valued content field. Anthropic tool_result blocks can carry `content` as an array
of content blocks (e.g., `[{ type: "text", text: "Structured output provided successfully" }]`).
The strict `===` check fails on array-shaped payloads, causing every schema-dispatched agent
to false-positive as truncated.

originalText: the judged action's `target` is the *parent's* resolved `aws.profile` (`scripts/agent-operator/src/steps/run-log-triage.ts:212`), but `triageRun`'s argv emits only `--preset=` and `--operation=analyze` (`scripts/agent-operator/src/lib/cli-surface.ts:475`), so the child resolves its own `aws.profile` independently — and a preset is forbidden from declaring one (`scripts/agent-operator/src/lib/triage-presets.ts:251`). Whenever the parent's profile came from anywhere other than the inherited `AWS_PROFILE` env var (its own CLI arg at precedence 1, or its config file at 6), the account actually queried is not the account the policy graded. This is the same divergence class `TRIAGE_OPERATION_TOKEN` was introduced to close for the verb, and `run-preset` sidesteps it only by refusing target scripts that declare `aws.profile`; pinning a `--aws.profile=<operatorProfile>` passthrough token would close it the same way.

Current line 623 shows triageRun appends `--aws.profile=${operation.operatorProfile}` to the child invocation, passing the operator's profile through to the child script with precedence level 1 (hard to override). The child script thus receives the parent's resolved profile, closing the divergence the finding described.
